solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: To the younger generation, lower capital has nothing for society (3-3)

indicatorNotes.for: one thing 'for' another stands in its place, so O replaces S

blocks.note: the standard abbreviation; this S is the one that goes

annotation.surface: A snooty remark that the young think the lower classes of the capital have nothing to offer society.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lower' looks like the opposite of upper, but it is one that lows; a moo-cow is what small children call a cow.
annotation.definitionFit: A cow lows, so it is a lower, and moo-cow is the nursery word young children use for it.

entries.clue: Antipodean case documents uncovered (5)

indicatorNotes.uncovered: taking the cover off a word strips its outside letters

blocks.note: a dossier is the file of papers on a case
the D at the front and the R at the back come off

annotation.surface: Papers about a case in Australia that have been exposed.
annotation.walkthrough: OSSIE is a less common spelling of Aussie.
annotation.definitionFit: Ossie, like Aussie, is informal for an Australian, someone from the Antipodes.

entries.clue: Rural nobleman stunned with horror when pet absconds (11)

indicatorNotes.with: one piece goes with the next, side by side
indicatorNotes.absconds: whoever absconds leaves, so PET is taken out of the word

blocks.note: a count is a European noble

annotation.surface: A country aristocrat left frozen with fear when the family pet runs off.
annotation.walkthrough: The pet's disappearance is the reason for the horror in the surface, and also the instruction to lift PET from PETRIFIED.
annotation.definitionFit: Countrified means having the manners or look of the countryside, that is rural.

entries.clue: Maybe poison militant shortly (8)

indicatorNotes.shortly: said shortly, the word is cut short by its last letter

annotation.surface: A militant who may soon turn to poison.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Shortly' reads as 'soon'; it means the word is clipped.
annotation.definitionFit: Warfarin is a blood thinner best known as rat poison, so it is one example of a poison.

entries.clue: Heads of light entertainment enthralled by past gag (7)

indicatorNotes.Heads of: the head of each word is its first letter
indicatorNotes.enthralled by: held captive by, so LE sits inside SINCE

blocks.note: first letters of Light and Entertainment

annotation.surface: Television executives captivated by an old joke.
annotation.walkthrough: Heads of Light Entertainment are BBC bosses in the surface; here they are just two initials.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: stopping someone speaking, by cloth or by order, is both to gag and to silence them.

entries.clue: Agreeable power mentioned guards (5)

indicatorNotes.guards: the word stands round the P, guarding it

annotation.surface: A pleasant power that has been talked about as a protector.
annotation.walkthrough: SAPID is a rare word for pleasant to the taste.
annotation.definitionFit: Sapid means having a pleasing flavour, and by extension agreeable.

entries.clue: Marine sheet drags — trouble follows (7)

indicatorNotes.follows: the second piece follows, coming after the first

blocks.note: to ail is to trouble, as in 'what ails you'

annotation.surface: A sailor hauling a sheet about while trouble dogs them.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sheet' in the surface is a rope or bedding; here it means a sail.
annotation.definitionFit: A lugsail is a four-cornered sail on a slanting yard, a sheet of canvas on a boat.

entries.clue: Sceptic “name” working to contradict stuck-up clergyman (11)

indicatorNotes.stuck-up: stuck up in a down clue, the word reads from the bottom

blocks.note: to belie is to show something false

annotation.surface: A so-called sceptic busy contradicting a snooty vicar.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stuck-up' reads as snooty; in a down clue it turns REV upwards.
annotation.definitionFit: A sceptic who doubts a claim is a nonbeliever in it.

entries.clue: Bird smothered in upset detergent (5)

indicatorNotes.smothered in: the bird lies buried inside the letters
indicatorNotes.upset: upset in a down clue, the letters run upwards

blocks.note: the letters t-e-g-r-e sit inside deTERGEnt
the five letters are read from the bottom up

annotation.surface: A bird drowned in a spilt pool of washing liquid.
annotation.walkthrough: An oil-spill picture; the reversal runs up the down entry.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by class: the egret is a small white heron of marshes and shores.

entries.clue: Nicked American alongside others framed by Communist (8)

indicatorNotes.alongside: one piece is placed beside the next
indicatorNotes.framed by: the inner word sits inside the outer, as in a frame

annotation.surface: An American and his comrades set up by a Communist.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Framed' is police language in the surface to fit 'Nicked'; here it means enclosed.
annotation.definitionFit: Nicked is British slang for arrested by the police.

entries.clue: Kind of Bible ambiguous surrounding origin of universe releasing energy (9)

indicatorNotes.surrounding: the word goes round the U
indicatorNotes.origin of: the origin of a word is its first letter
indicatorNotes.releasing: letting E go takes it out

annotation.surface: A take on the Bible that is vague about how the universe began and how its energy was released.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Kind of Bible' reads as one phrase; 'Kind' is the definition and 'of' a link.
annotation.definitionFit: Avuncular means kind and genial, like a favourite uncle.

entries.clue: Set right prior to brief farewell (5)

indicatorNotes.prior to: prior to means earlier than, so the letter for right is placed before the farewell
indicatorNotes.brief: a brief word is cut short at the end

annotation.surface: Putting something right just before a quick goodbye.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Set right' reads as one verb; 'Set' is the definition, a wireless set.
annotation.definitionFit: Set here is the old word for a receiver, as in wireless set or TV set, so a radio is one.

entries.clue: Traditional newspaper promotion split either side of excessive hype, extremely boring to begin with (4,3,4)

annotation.type: container + charade + last letter + first letter

indicatorNotes.either side of: the word splits and its halves sit on either side of the rest
indicatorNotes.extremely: the extremes of a word are its first and last letters
indicatorNotes.to begin with: the letter that begins the word

blocks.note: to spall is to split or chip off, of stone
first and last letters of Hype

annotation.surface: A newspaper's old promotion divided opinion, flanked by hype and dull from the start.
annotation.walkthrough: SPALL is a stonemason's word; spot the ball was a long-running British newspaper competition in which readers marked where the ball had been erased from a football photo.
annotation.definitionFit: Spot the ball was a prize competition that newspapers ran for decades, so a traditional newspaper promotion.

entries.clue: Mournful English and Gaelic broadcast (7)

indicatorNotes.and: one piece and then the next
indicatorNotes.broadcast: scattered about, as seed is broadcast

annotation.surface: A sad programme aired in English and Gaelic.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' fits the radio picture, but here it scatters GAELIC.
annotation.definitionFit: Elegiac means in the mood of an elegy, a lament, so mournful.

entries.clue: Conservative duffed up one long-haired misfit (6,3,2,1,5,4)

annotation.answer: SQUARE PEG IN A ROUND HOLE

indicatorNotes.duffed: duffed up means beaten up, so the letters are knocked about

annotation.surface: A conservative type beats up a long-haired outsider.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Duffed up' reads as a phrasal verb; the indicator is 'duffed' alone and 'up' is part of the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: A square peg in a round hole is someone who does not fit their situation, a misfit.

entries.clue: Eg Russell T Davies’s first barren broadcast (8)

indicatorNotes.broadcast: scattered about, as seed is broadcast

blocks.note: the T of the name, used as it stands

annotation.surface: A barren programme by Russell T Davies, the television writer.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface runs 'Russell T Davies' as one name, the Doctor Who writer; the break comes after Russell, which is Bertrand Russell, the philosopher.
annotation.definitionFit: Bertrand is the first name of the philosopher Bertrand Russell, one Russell among others.

entries.clue: Checking short month, current account’s squeaky clean (7)

indicatorNotes.Checking: to check something is to hold it in, so AC holds the rest

blocks.note: AC is the usual abbreviation for account, and the ’s stands for has

annotation.surface: Going over a month's current account statement and finding it spotless.
annotation.walkthrough: The order reverses the surface: it is the account that does the checking, and "current" is a physics symbol, not a type of bank account.
annotation.definitionFit: Aseptic means free of germs, so surgically, squeakily clean.

entries.clue: For some, neat ending when in a stew? (6)

annotation.definition: For some, neat ending when in a stew?

blocks.note: neat is an old word for cattle
a tail is the end part

annotation.surface: A tidy conclusion when someone is in a flap.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Neat' is the old word for cattle, and 'in a stew' is not panic but a pot: oxtail is often stewed.
annotation.definitionFit: Oxtail is literally the end of a neat, and many people eat it in a stew.

entries.clue: Mock frail cat I repeatedly bothered (10)

indicatorNotes.repeatedly: I is used more than once, here twice
indicatorNotes.bothered: shaken up, so the letters are mixed

blocks.note: anagram fodder, with I taken twice

annotation.surface: Teasing a frail cat until it keeps getting upset.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mock' reads as a verb for teasing; it is the adjective, as in mock leather.
annotation.definitionFit: Mock and artificial both mean imitation, not the real thing.

entries.clue: Mechanical sort of grooving tool among electronic drills (9)

indicatorNotes.among: among means in the middle of, which is the word IN itself
indicatorNotes.drills: the letters drill into the tool, going inside it

blocks.note: a router cuts grooves in wood

annotation.surface: A mechanical kind of grooving tool among some electric drills.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mechanical sort of grooving tool' reads as one description of a machine; 'sort' means a person.
annotation.definitionFit: A routineer is someone who sticks to routine, a person who acts mechanically.

entries.clue: Flower arranging in general mostly trite (7)

indicatorNotes.mostly: most of the word, all but its last letter

annotation.surface: A view that flower arranging is on the whole rather dull.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In general' reads as 'on the whole'; 'in' is a link and 'general' is Ike.
annotation.definitionFit: The Japanese name for the formal art of arranging cut flowers, borrowed into English.

entries.clue: Duke escapes poverty crushing utter dope (12)

indicatorNotes.escapes: the D escapes, leaving the word
indicatorNotes.crushing: the outer word crushes the inner one inside it

annotation.surface: A duke escaping poverty flattens a total idiot.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dope' reads as a fool, and 'utter' as total; dope is information and utter is a verb.
annotation.definitionFit: Dope is slang for inside information, which is intelligence.

entries.clue: Fairly good Hispanic cheer ahead of Republican being welcomed by panel (9)

indicatorNotes.ahead of: ahead of means in front of, so the cheer is placed before the letter for Republican
indicatorNotes.being welcomed by: taken in by the outer word

blocks.note: a panel or board, as in a round table

annotation.surface: A decent Spanish cheer for a Republican greeted by a committee.
annotation.walkthrough: A panel of experts is a table in the sense of a round-table discussion.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the lukewarm sense: tolerable food is neither bad nor great, just fairly good.

entries.clue: Soldiers protected by cover step up (8)

indicatorNotes.protected by: something protected by a cover sits inside it

blocks.note: incase is a variant spelling of encase, to cover

annotation.surface: Troops shielded by covering fire move forward.
annotation.walkthrough: RE, the Royal Engineers, is a British army corps and a standard crossword source of 'soldiers'.
annotation.definitionFit: A verb phrase synonym: to step up production is to raise or increase it.

entries.clue: Peak fitness upped jogging intensity primarily (4)

indicatorNotes.primarily: primarily means first of all, so each word gives its first letter

blocks.note: first letters of the four words

annotation.surface: Peak fitness comes mainly from running harder.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Peak fitness' reads as one phrase; the mountain is the definition and fitness is the first word of the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Mount Fuji is Japan's highest peak.

entries.clue: Pawn waving cleaver assassinated PM (8)

indicatorNotes.waving: a cleaver being waved about is moving, so its letters move too

annotation.surface: A pawn brandishing a meat cleaver kills a prime minister.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface's weapon is a red herring: Spencer Perceval was shot in the House of Commons lobby in 1812.
annotation.definitionFit: Spencer Perceval is the only British prime minister to have been assassinated.

entries.clue: Off and on, warm sirocco scattered plant (9)

indicatorNotes.Off and on: off and on means every other one, so alternate letters are kept
indicatorNotes.scattered: scattered letters are strewn about into a new order

blocks.note: the second and fourth letters of wArM

annotation.surface: A hot desert wind that blows fitfully and scatters seed.
annotation.walkthrough: The sirocco is a hot Mediterranean wind, so 'off and on, warm' reads as its weather; the plant hides at the very end.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by class: crocosmia, or montbretia, is a garden plant with sprays of orange flowers.

entries.clue: Historic hardship reduced great cricketer (8)

indicatorNotes.reduced: cut down at both ends, leaving only the letters in the middle of the phrase

blocks.note: the letters run from histoRIC into HARDShip

annotation.surface: A great player of old brought low by hard times.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a fallen star; 'reduced' trims HISTO and HIP from the two words.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Sir Viv Richards, the West Indies batsman, is one of the greatest cricketers.

entries.clue: Fool breaking unopened zip interrupts pretty walk (9)

indicatorNotes.breaking: the fool breaks into the zip, landing inside it
indicatorNotes.unopened: not opened, so the word loses its first letter
indicatorNotes.interrupts: the group cuts into the middle of the last word

annotation.surface: An idiot's broken zip spoils an attractive stroll.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Walk' looks like a stroll; it is the informal verb for things going missing, as in 'my pen has walked'.
annotation.definitionFit: An informal sense: when things walk, they go missing, so they disappear.

entries.clue: Big shop boosted work inspired by fashion designer Jean and setter (8)

indicatorNotes.boosted: boosted means lifted, and in a down clue lifting runs the letters upwards
indicatorNotes.inspired by: breathed in by, so OP goes inside

blocks.note: Jean Muir, the British fashion designer
the setter refers to themself as me

annotation.surface: A department store's hit collection, inspired by Jean Muir and the crossword setter.
annotation.walkthrough: Jean Muir was a British designer known for fluid jersey dresses; 'boosted' covers the whole assembly, not just the work.
annotation.definitionFit: An emporium is a grand word for a large store, a big shop.

entries.clue: Peccadillo made Monsieur angry (12)

indicatorNotes.angry: an angry person is stirred up, and so are these letters

annotation.surface: A little slip that made a Frenchman cross.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Monsieur' looks like a French definition or abbreviation (M); every letter is fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: A near synonym: a peccadillo is a small sin, and a misdemeanour a minor wrongdoing.

entries.clue: Start to realise how Jersey is not without purpose (10)

indicatorNotes.Start to: the start of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: a Jersey is a dairy cow, which is never lacking an udder

annotation.surface: Beginning to see that Jersey life has no direction.
annotation.walkthrough: Jersey looks like the Channel Island or the jumper; it is the dairy breed, which has an udder, so it is not udderless.
annotation.definitionFit: Figurative: a ship with no rudder cannot be steered, so rudderless means drifting without purpose.

entries.clue: Jacket that’s suggested by tourist on vacation? (7)

indicatorNotes.on vacation: a vacated word has been emptied, leaving only its first and last letters

blocks.note: emptying tourist leaves the T at each end, and that pair of T letters is spoken of as a double one

annotation.surface: A coat that a holidaymaker might bring to mind.
annotation.walkthrough: The two letters left are not written out; they are described, so TT is read as 'double T'.
annotation.definitionFit: A doublet is a close-fitting man's jacket of the Tudor era.

entries.clue: Complaint by Dorothy’s companion eating mum’s fruit (4,6)

indicatorNotes.by: one piece is set by, beside, the next
indicatorNotes.eating: the dog eats MA, which ends up inside it

blocks.note: Toto, Dorothy's dog in The Wizard of Oz

annotation.surface: A gripe that Dorothy's little dog is eating mum's fruit.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mum's fruit' reads as one possession; the fruit is the definition standing alone.
annotation.definitionFit: Botanically a tomato is a fruit, and the beef tomato is a large variety.

entries.clue: British journalism’s fast track? (5,6)

blocks.note: the definition in its straight sense: the national press
fleet means fast and a street is a track, read word by word

annotation.surface: The quickest route to a career in the British press.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fast track' reads as a career shortcut; take it literally, a swift road, and the London street of the newspapers appears.
annotation.definitionFit: Metonymy: Fleet Street in London was home to the national newspapers, so its name stands for British journalism.

entries.clue: Second coach’s taking on island tours, those with a twist? (6,6)

indicatorNotes.taking on: the coach takes the island on board, so I goes inside

blocks.note: a mo is a moment, a second
a bus, a coach, with its 's

annotation.surface: A second coach picks up passengers on an island tour with a surprise ending.
annotation.walkthrough: The 's of coach's is kept as a letter; a Möbius strip is a loop of paper with a half-twist, giving one side only.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by description: each Möbius strip is made by giving a band of paper a half-twist.

entries.clue: Yuppy periodically tense in 30 days addicted to surreal comic collection? (5,6)

indicatorNotes.periodically: at regular intervals, so every other letter is taken
indicatorNotes.in: the letters go in the month
indicatorNotes.addicted to: someone addicted to a thing is on it, giving ON

blocks.note: the first, third and fifth letters of Yuppy

annotation.surface: A yuppy who spends a month hooked on surreal comics.
annotation.walkthrough: Monty Python was a British comedy group; as a group of comics it is a collection, hence the question mark.
annotation.definitionFit: Monty Python was a troupe of surreal comedians, a collection of comics.

entries.clue: Tory influence stifling Foreign Office over land-access permissions (6,2,3)

indicatorNotes.stifling: to stifle is to smother, closing round what is inside
indicatorNotes.over: turned over, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: to hold sway is to have influence

annotation.surface: Conservative sway blocks the Foreign Office on questions of public access.
annotation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' could mean placed above; here it reverses FO before it goes in.
annotation.definitionFit: Rights of way are the legal permissions to cross someone's land by a path.

entries.clue: Perhaps sample fried eggs every so often, almost 50 to go round (4,4)

indicatorNotes.every so often: at intervals, so alternate letters are kept
indicatorNotes.almost: almost the whole word, so the last letter is dropped
indicatorNotes.to go round: the number goes round the eggs

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters of friedeggs

annotation.surface: Trying out some fried eggs now and then, with fifty going round.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' signals that a sample is one example of a free gift.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a product sample handed out is one kind of free gift.

entries.clue: Drunken online nuisance carefully looked at (9)

annotation.surface: A drunken internet troll was watched closely.
annotation.walkthrough: Trolleyed is British slang for very drunk.
annotation.definitionFit: Regional slang: in Britain, someone trolleyed is so drunk they might need wheeling home.

entries.clue: Film star Leonard rejected large car stores (8)

indicatorNotes.rejected: thrown back, so the name is read backwards
indicatorNotes.stores: the car stores the letters inside itself

blocks.note: the Mini, the small British car

annotation.surface: A film star named Leonard was turned down, and a large car keeps the rest.
annotation.walkthrough: Liza Minnelli is the star; 'large car' looks like one phrase but the car is a Mini.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Liza Minnelli, the star of Cabaret, is a film star.

entries.clue: With a little work from the east, expanded (4)

indicatorNotes.from the east: on a map east is on the right, so reading from the east runs right to left

blocks.note: the erg is a tiny unit of work in physics
the standard abbreviation, as in w/

annotation.surface: Something that grew bigger with a small amount of work in the east.
annotation.walkthrough: The W comes first in the clue but last in the answer: only 'a little work' is read from the east.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something that grew got bigger, that is expanded.

entries.clue: Environmentalist fine consuming dash of Cockburn’s Port (8)

indicatorNotes.consuming: the word eats the letter, taking it inside
indicatorNotes.dash of: a dash is a small amount, here just the first letter

blocks.note: a Green, a member of an ecology party

annotation.surface: A green campaigner is happy to drink a drop of Cockburn's port.
annotation.walkthrough: Cockburn's is a brand of port wine, so 'Port' reads as the drink; it is a Scottish port town on the Clyde.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Greenock is a port on the Firth of Clyde in Scotland.

entries.clue: Perverse unintroduced rate cuts occurring now (12)

indicatorNotes.unintroduced: a word not introduced loses the letter that introduces it, its first
indicatorNotes.cuts: the letters cut into the word, landing in its middle

blocks.note: TEMPO, a rate, with its T taken off

annotation.surface: Perverse, unannounced interest-rate cuts happening today.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rate cuts' reads as a money phrase; 'rate' belongs with 'unintroduced' and 'cuts' is the container instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: contemporary means of the present time, occurring now.

entries.clue: Missing out at first, shut down and restart company backing for one month (7)

indicatorNotes.Missing: a missing letter is left out
indicatorNotes.at first: the first letter of out, an O
indicatorNotes.backing: backing moves backwards, so the whole string is reversed

blocks.note: one O, the first letter of out, goes

annotation.surface: Missing out at first, a company shuts down and restarts, with backing for one month.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Missing out at first' sits at the front of the clue but applies to REBOOT: only one of its two O letters goes.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: October is one month of the year.

entries.clue: US unit engaged in northern river works? (10)

blocks.note: at = engaged in, as in 'at work'
the Ure, a river in Yorkshire, northern England

annotation.surface: An American unit busy on some works on a northern river.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Works' looks like engineering on a river; it means written works, hence the question mark.
annotation.definitionFit: A collective noun: literature is the whole body of written works.

entries.clue: They swarm a great deal, covering most of point (7)

indicatorNotes.covering: the outer word covers the inner one, which goes inside
indicatorNotes.most of: most of the word, all but its last letter

blocks.note: CUSP, a point, without its P

annotation.surface: Creatures that crowd in their thousands, covering most of a headland.
annotation.walkthrough: A cusp is a point, as of a tooth or a crescent moon.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by description: locusts are the grasshoppers that gather in vast swarms.

entries.clue: Rank of university within quantitative data (6)

indicatorNotes.within: U goes within the other word, inside it

annotation.surface: A university's position in the league tables, found in its statistics.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rank of university' reads as one phrase; 'of' is a link.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: status is standing or position, one's rank.

entries.clue: Cane sons, more or less full of whiskey (5)

indicatorNotes.full of: the letters fill the outer word, sitting inside it

blocks.note: -ish, as in 'six-ish', means more or less
W is whiskey in the NATO alphabet

annotation.surface: Beating sons who are more or less full of whiskey.
annotation.walkthrough: Whiskey is the NATO phonetic word for W, which is why it is spelt with an E.
annotation.definitionFit: A verb synonym: to cane someone is to thrash them with a rod, which is to swish them.

entries.clue: Dip picked up on cheek and mouth on TV? (3-4)

indicatorNotes.picked up: sounds picked up by the ear, so the word is heard, not spelt

annotation.surface: Dipping a cheek and mouth on television.
annotation.walkthrough: The order is swapped: the heard piece is written first but comes second. 'Mouth' is the verb, as in mouthing words to a recording.
annotation.definitionFit: A performer on TV who mouths along to a recording is miming, which is to lip-sync.

entries.clue: Assume one will stop job (5)

indicatorNotes.will stop: the letter stops up the word like a plug, going inside it

annotation.surface: Supposing that someone will quit their job.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stop' reads as quitting; it means plugging a gap, as in stopping a hole.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to posit something is to put it forward as true, to assume it.

entries.clue: Brings back old academic, a dinosaur (8)

blocks.note: a university teacher at Oxford or Cambridge

annotation.surface: An old professor dismissed as a dinosaur.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Brings back' reads as a phrasal verb and 'old academic, a dinosaur' as an insult; 'back' reverses only GETS.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose sense: the stegodon was a prehistoric elephant, not strictly a dinosaur, but just as extinct.

entries.clue: Southern republic’s tanks supporting submarine manoeuvres? (5)

annotation.surface: A southern republic's army tanks backing naval submarine exercises.
annotation.walkthrough: Tanks and submarine manoeuvres suggest the military; the tanks are air tanks and the manoeuvres are a diver's underwater moves.
annotation.definitionFit: Scuba gear is the air tanks that let a diver move about underwater.

entries.clue: Playwright somehow or other found inspiration in seconds (5)

indicatorNotes.in seconds: the letters sit in second place in each word

blocks.note: the second letter of each of the five words

annotation.surface: A dramatist who somehow found inspiration in a flash.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In seconds' reads as 'very quickly'; it tells you to take second letters. Joe Orton was an English playwright.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Joe Orton wrote the black comedies Loot and Entertaining Mr Sloane.

entries.clue: Saw, from Hamlet, how to verify subtitles I translated (7,2,3,4,2,3)

annotation.answer: BREVITY IS THE SOUL OF WIT

indicatorNotes.translated: translated text is turned into something else, so the letters are rearranged

annotation.surface: A foreign film buff checking the subtitles of Hamlet.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Saw' looks like a tool or a past tense; it is an old saying. Polonius says the line in Hamlet, ironically, at great length.
annotation.definitionFit: A saw is an old saying, and this one is spoken by Polonius in Hamlet.

entries.clue: Poor wife was sick (8)

annotation.surface: A poor wife who felt ill.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Poor wife' reads as pity for her; 'Poor' stands alone as the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the pitiable sense: a poor soul is a wretched one.

entries.clue: Coastal country is beginning to improve fish nets (7)

indicatorNotes.beginning to: the beginning of a word is its first letter
indicatorNotes.nets: a fish that nets something catches it inside

annotation.surface: A seaside nation's fishing starts to pick up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fish nets' reads as a noun; it is a fish netting the letters, reversing the surface's roles.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Tunisia is a North African country on the Mediterranean coast.

entries.clue: Lackey in gang partly vandalising estate, say (6)

indicatorNotes.partly: only part of the phrase is used, the letters inside it

blocks.note: the letters run from lacKEY through IN to Gang

annotation.surface: A gang's hanger-on who wrecks property on a housing estate.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Estate' reads as a housing estate; it is an estate car, the British word for a station wagon, and keying is scratching its paint with a key.
annotation.definitionFit: Keying a car means gouging its paintwork with a key, a common act of vandalism.
